questions.question_text: Which prism has the same volume as $2\times3\times7$ cm?

options.why: Adds $1$ to the width and subtracts $1$ from the height, assuming this preserves volume. It preserves the sum of the dimensions, but $2\times4\times6=48$, not $42$.
Changes the length from $2$ to $3$ and the height from $7$ to $5$ without checking that the changes preserve the product: $3\times3\times5=45$, not $42$.
Adds the dimensions incorrectly as $12$, then assumes equal sums mean equal volumes. In fact, $1+5+8=14$, while $2+3+7=12$, and $1\times5\times8=40$, not $42$.

questions.question_text: Do $4\times4\times3$ cm and $2\times6\times4$ cm prisms have equal volumes?

options.why: Compares individual dimensions instead of their products.
Assumes the longer dimension guarantees greater volume.

options.text: No; their volumes are $11\text{ cm}^3$ and $12\text{ cm}^3$.
options.why: Adds each prism’s three dimensions instead of multiplying them: $4+4+3=11$ and $2+6+4=12$.

questions.question_text: Complete the dimensions for equal volumes: $3\times4\times5=2\times5\times x$.

options.why: Copies the other prism’s height without checking the product.
Divides the target volume $60$ by $5$ only and forgets the other known factor $2$.
Uses the first prism’s length as the missing factor.

options.text: Different dimensions can produce the same volume.
Equal-volume prisms must have equal lengths.
options.why: Assumes one dimension must match even though only the product must match.

options.text: The tallest prism always has the greatest volume.
options.why: Uses height alone and ignores length and width.

options.text: Changing any dimension never changes volume.
options.why: Ignores that the product changes unless another dimension compensates.

questions.solution_text: Volume depends on the product, so different factor triples can match.

questions.question_text: Which dimension triple gives a prism with volume $72\text{ cm}^3$?

options.why: Uses $5$ as the height by incorrectly calculating $72\div(3\times4)$ as $5$ instead of $6$. These dimensions give $60\text{ cm}^3$.
Divides $72$ by $2\times5=10$ and discards the remainder $2$, choosing height $7$. These dimensions give $70\text{ cm}^3$.
Divides $72$ by $4\times4=16$ to get $4.5$, then rounds the height up to $5$ even though the volume must match exactly. These dimensions give $80\text{ cm}^3$.

questions.question_text: Prism A is $2\times5\times8$ m. Prism B has length $4$ m and width $5$ m. What height gives equal volume?

options.why: Copies prism A’s first dimension instead of preserving the product.
Copies prism A’s height and doubles the volume.
Divides the target volume by the width only.
